kid.question: Which two cities are named at the start of Micah's message?

options.text: Nineveh and Babylon
Tyre and Sidon
Samaria and Jerusalem
Jericho and Bethlehem

kid.explanation: Micah's opening identifies Samaria and Jerusalem as the cities concerning which he received the Lord's word.

kid.question: What happens to Samaria's idols?

options.text: They are broken to pieces
They are carried to Egypt
They are buried under trees
They are sold to traders

kid.explanation: The Lord says Samaria's graven images will be beaten to pieces and its idols laid desolate.

kid.question: Why does Micah tell the people to mourn for their children?

options.text: Their children have died in battle
Their children are trapped by famine
Their children have fled into hiding
Their children have been taken captive

kid.explanation: The call to mourning is explained by the children's departure into captivity.

kid.question: What do the people who plan evil take from others?

options.text: Their boats and fishing nets
Their fields and houses
Their sheep and cattle
Their silver and gold

kid.explanation: Those who plot evil covet fields and houses and take them by violence.

kid.question: When do these people carry out the wrong they planned?

options.text: When evening shadows fall
When morning becomes light
When the harvest is finished
When the Sabbath is over

kid.explanation: They devise evil on their beds and put it into practice when morning comes because they have the power to do so.

kid.question: What happens to the women mentioned in Micah 2:9?

options.text: They are taken from their vineyards
They are driven from the marketplace
They are turned from the sanctuary
They are forced from their homes

kid.explanation: Micah condemns the eviction of women from their pleasant houses and the harm done to their children.

kid.question: What animals picture the people the Lord will gather?

options.text: Sheep in a fold
Birds in a nest
Fish in a net
Oxen in a stall

kid.explanation: The Lord promises to gather Israel's remnant like sheep together in their fold.

kid.question: Who will be at the head of the gathered people?

options.text: The priest
The seer
The Lord
The captain

kid.explanation: Their king passes before them and the Lord is at their head as they go through the gate.

kid.question: What happens when the cruel rulers cry to the Lord?

options.text: He hides His face from them
He sends a famine upon them
He takes their kingdom from them
He scatters them among foreign peoples

kid.explanation: The Lord will not hear them and will hide His face because of their evil deeds.

kid.question: What does Micah say gives him power to speak?

options.text: The advice of the king
The Spirit of the Lord
The teaching of the priests
The support of the people

kid.explanation: Micah says he is full of power by the Spirit of the Lord to declare Israel's sin.

high-school.question: How does Micah connect Samaria's wound with Judah?

options.text: The wound has reached Judah, even Jerusalem's gate
The wound has driven Judah's people into the wilderness
The wound has cut Judah off from neighboring allies
The wound has left Judah's royal family in captivity

high-school.explanation: The incurable wound has come to Judah and reached even Jerusalem's gate, extending the warning beyond Samaria.

high-school.question: What reason introduces the threatened destruction of Samaria?

options.text: Samaria's broken alliance with the kings of Judah
The rulers' refusal to surrender to the invading army
Jacob's transgression and the sins of Israel's house
The people's abandonment of their fields and vineyards

high-school.explanation: Israel's transgression introduces the threat to make Samaria a heap, pour its stones into the valley, and expose its foundations.

high-school.question: How does Micah describe the timing and motive of property seizure?

options.text: Sudden famine becomes public trading approved by priests
Evening mourning becomes morning migration ordered by kings
Harvest disputes become land exchanges settled by judges
Nighttime plotting becomes morning action backed by power

high-school.explanation: The offenders plan on their beds, act at daylight because they can, and seize coveted fields and houses.

high-school.question: What loss does the lament following the land-seizure accusation describe?

options.text: The people's harvest is burned and their vineyards left without workers
The people's portion is changed and their fields divided away
The people's houses are flooded and their wells filled with stones
The people's grain is seized and their livestock driven into the wilderness

high-school.explanation: Seizure of another's heritage is followed by lament over their own portion being changed and fields divided away.

high-school.question: What treatment of peaceful travelers makes the people resemble an enemy?

options.text: They strip clothing from unsuspecting passersby
They levy tolls on caravans entering the city
They force travelers to serve in the army
They send visitors back across the border

high-school.explanation: Micah calls his people an enemy because they pull garments from those passing securely and averse to war.

high-school.question: What message would make a lying speaker welcome among these people?

options.text: A promise of silver and gold
A promise of abundant crops and livestock
A promise of victory and foreign tribute
A prophecy of wine and strong drink

high-school.explanation: Micah says a lying man who prophesied wine and strong drink would be the prophet this people wanted.

high-school.question: How does the end of Micah 2 change the picture after the command to depart?

options.text: The Lord replaces the remnant with neighboring peoples
The Lord scatters the remnant beyond another border
The Lord gathers a remnant and leads them out
The Lord leaves the remnant under foreign command

high-school.explanation: After polluted rest and departure, the Lord promises to assemble the remnant like a flock and stand at its head.

high-school.question: What does Micah explicitly ask Israel's heads and princes to know?

options.text: Judgment
Genealogies
Boundaries
Prophecies

high-school.explanation: Micah asks whether the heads and princes should know judgment before portraying their treatment of the people as butchery.

high-school.question: What determines the corrupt prophets' message of peace or war?

options.text: Whether someone belongs to the royal family
Whether someone supplies them with food
Whether someone has returned from captivity
Whether someone serves at the temple altar

high-school.explanation: The prophets cry peace while they have something to bite, but prepare war against someone who puts nothing in their mouths.

high-school.question: What wrong does Micah name in his closing appeal to Israel's heads and princes?

options.text: They abandon the gates and neglect the walls
They sell inherited fields and confiscate the vineyards
They abhor judgment and pervert equity
They hide foreign soldiers and protect their commanders

high-school.explanation: Micah addresses the heads and princes as those who abhor judgment and pervert all equity.

expert.question: What role does the temple have in Micah's opening summons?

options.text: The Lord orders its restoration as a refuge for the hearers
The Lord appears from it as a witness against the hearers
The Lord assigns its priests to negotiate with the hearers
The Lord promises its wealth as compensation for the hearers

expert.explanation: Earth and peoples are summoned to hear as the Lord witnesses against them from His holy temple and comes down.

expert.question: What do wax before fire and water on a steep slope illustrate?

options.text: Armies retreating and refugees scattering before Samaria's rulers
Idols burning and treasures spilling from the temple's chambers
Mountains melting and valleys splitting at the Lord's coming
Fields flooding and vineyards collapsing after autumn's rainfall

expert.explanation: The images describe mountains melting and valleys cleaving beneath the descending Lord, rather than a military maneuver or seasonal storm.

expert.question: How does the repeated Jerusalem-gate language shape Micah 1:9-12?

options.text: It brings threatened harm to the center of Judah's life
It sends surviving exiles toward the center of temple worship
It marks completed repairs to the center of Judah's defenses
It places Samaria's rulers at the center of peace negotiations

expert.explanation: Both the wound reaching Judah and the evil for which Maroth waited end at Jerusalem's gate.

expert.question: What verbal reversal links the offenders' plans with the Lord's response?

options.text: Their gathering captives is answered by His gathering armies
Their dividing tribute is answered by His dividing kingdoms
Their building houses is answered by His building strongholds
Their devising evil is answered by His devising calamity

expert.explanation: Those who devise iniquity hear the Lord say He devises evil against this family, reversing the direction of their planning.

expert.question: What qualification accompanies the claim that the Lord's words do good?

options.text: They do good to the one who supplies the prophets
They do good to the one who commands the chariots
They do good to the one who walks uprightly
They do good to the one who owns the inheritance

expert.explanation: Amid resistance to prophecy, the question specifies the person walking uprightly as the recipient of the words' good.

expert.question: How do the accusations against travelers and women broaden the property indictment?

options.text: They add unpaid tribute and damage to city walls
They add stolen clothing and expulsion from homes
They add withheld harvests and neglect of public roads
They add broken treaties and refusal of military service

expert.explanation: The charge extends from fields and houses to robbing peaceful travelers of garments and evicting women from pleasant homes.

expert.question: How does the flock image lead into the gate scene?

options.text: Gathered people stay enclosed while their king seeks allies
Gathered people pass out with their king before them
Scattered people return secretly while their king remains captive
Scattered people join invaders while their king abandons Zion

expert.explanation: The remnant is assembled like a flock; a breaker precedes their passage through the gate, with their king before them and the Lord at their head.

expert.question: What response will the Lord make when the rulers later cry to Him?

options.text: He will hide His face because of their evil deeds
He will appoint a new prophet to reveal their hidden offenses
He will demand a larger sacrifice before addressing their complaint
He will replace their judges before hearing the case against them

expert.explanation: After the grotesque image of rulers consuming the people, verse 4 explicitly grounds the hidden face in their evil conduct.

expert.question: How do night and sunset function in the oracle against mercenary prophets?

options.text: They designate the hour appointed for a new revelation
They conceal the route prepared for the prophets' escape
They mark the time appointed for the prophets' sacrifice
They picture loss of vision and of an answer from God

expert.explanation: Night, darkness, and sunset are explained by the lack of vision, divination, and an answer from God.

expert.question: What pairing defines Micah's empowerment and task in contrast with the corrupt prophets?

options.text: The Lord's Spirit and the declaration of transgression
The king's commission and the defense of the capital
The priests' instruction and the regulation of offerings
The elders' approval and the distribution of inheritance

expert.explanation: Against prophets whose messages depend on food, Micah claims power by the Lord's Spirit to declare sin and address rulers who pervert equity.
